questions.short_title: Ditch lights and sirens for fall-alarm calls
questions.question: After dispatch of medical-alert (PERS) activations changed to non-lights-and-siren response, how often did crews need to upgrade to a lights-and-siren transport?
options: About 1% of calls
About 12% of calls
About 5% of calls
About 0.2% of calls
questions.explanation: Only 4 of 1,628 post-change calls (0.2%) needed an L&S transport, and just one of those required advanced interventions. Remember this was a single-agency before-after study with no control group, so it's hypothesis-generating rather than proof the change is safe.

questions.short_title: Predicting outcomes in PEA cardiac arrest
questions.question: In PEA cardiac arrest, what did the study find about conversion to a shockable rhythm before hospital arrival?
options: It predicted good outcome only in cardiac PEA and worse outcome in non-cardiac PEA
It made no difference to neurological outcome in any group
It predicted good neurological outcome regardless of the cause of the arrest
It predicted worse outcome only when the arrest was unwitnessed
questions.explanation: Rhythm conversion predicted a favourable outcome in cardiac PEA but a poorer one in non-cardiac PEA. This is a registry association with presumed aetiology, so it generates hypotheses rather than proving causation.

questions.question: Between 2010 and 2023, national Australian data showed alcohol consumption declining by survey and wastewater measures. What happened to alcohol-related harms such as ambulance attendances over the same period?
options: They stayed roughly stable
They fell sharply after 2019
They increased substantially
They declined in line with consumption
questions.explanation: Most harm measures, including ambulance attendances, rose substantially even as consumption declined. The caveat is that these are population-level indicators, so no individual presentations were linked and the differing measures are hard to align.

questions.short_title: Feedback device lifts paediatric ventilation quality
questions.question: In this simulation study, a real-time ventilation feedback device had its largest effect on which measure of paediatric ventilation quality?
options: Mask seal, with leak under 30% far more often
Tidal volume, with guideline-adherent breaths jumping from 16.2% to 87%
Reducing gastric insufflation during bagging
Ventilation rate, with adherence rising from 65% to 88.6%
questions.explanation: The biggest jump was tidal volume adherence, from 16.2% to 87% of breaths, ahead of the improvements in rate and mask leak. Remember it's a manikin study — no patient outcomes, and real paediatric airways are less forgiving.

questions.short_title: Dispatcher training + volunteer app lifts bystander CPR
questions.question: Despite more bystanders starting CPR after the dispatcher training and volunteer app intervention, what did the trial find about patient outcomes?
options: Survival to discharge improved but neurological outcomes did not
Neither survival to discharge nor neurological outcomes improved
Survival to discharge and neurological outcomes improved alongside CPR rates
Outcomes improved only when CPR was started within 60 seconds
questions.explanation: The rise in bystander CPR did not translate into better survival or neurological outcomes, and the CPR effect itself lost significance under some statistical adjustments. So the results are hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing.

questions.short_title: Real-time feedback tidies BVM ventilation in arrest
questions.question: In the VECARS-2 study, real-time feedback improved insufflated-volume adherence to 68% of breaths in range. What happened to expired tidal volume?
options: It rose well above the guideline range
It matched the insufflated volume closely
It fell below the guideline range
It stayed essentially unchanged
questions.explanation: Expired tidal volumes were in range in only 14% vs 15% of breaths, so despite tidier insufflated volumes the air actually reaching the lungs didn't change. The before-and-after design without randomisation also means the findings are hypothesis-generating only.

questions.short_title: Resilience as a skill, not a trait
questions.question: In this study, 'work mode' was described as having a phased structure. Which phases did the authors identify?
options: Readiness, immersion and discharge
Preparation, containment and recovery
Anticipation, action and reflection
Alert, response and debrief
questions.explanation: Work mode moved through preparation, containment and recovery, showing features of skilled performance like an athlete's game face. Keep in mind the sample was small, drawn from a single service, and the interviewers analysed their own data.

questions.short_title: Dutch TEAM tool validated for resus training
questions.question: When using a validated TEAM-style tool to rate team performance in resus simulation, how many independent raters does the evidence suggest you need for good reliability?
options: Four raters, as reliability keeps rising steeply with each extra rater
Three raters, because two gives only moderate reliability
One rater is enough if they are an experienced instructor
Two raters give good reliability; three add little
questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability was good with three raters (ICC 0.78) but only moderate with two (ICC 0.68). Scores also clustered near the top, with ceiling effects on every item.
